summary: A remote Unimak Island light lit in 1903, destroyed with its five-man Coast Guard crew by the 1946 Aleutian tsunami.

lens.note: First order bivalve lens, installed 1904 (Society's record).

structures.note: Original light; a museum caption shows it standing behind the 1940 tower.
Destroyed by the tsunami of 1 April 1946; the foundation was all that was left.
Present tower per the Society's record.

staffing.note: Museum caption: an automated light built after the tsunami to replace the manned light. No year given in the sources read.

access.note: The Society's record lists it as not open to the public.

aton.note: The Society's record: Active Aid to Navigation? No.

events.note: Light put in place in 1903 (Senate tribute); the Society's record gives 1903 as the station's established year.
Original optic, a first order bivalve, per the Society's record.
Air diaphone installed in place of a siren or whistle, per the fiscal 1917 Commissioner's report.
Estimates proposed a flashing lens in place of the fixed one, and shore protection; a proposal, not confirmed as carried out.
Radio telephones planned for Scotch Cap and Cape Sarichef, to be installed that summer; installation not confirmed.
Radiobeacon established at Scotch Cap, per the Lighthouse Service Bulletin.
New concrete tower; described as a new concrete lighthouse built in 1940 (museum caption) and as Art Deco (Society).
Tower destroyed and all five crew killed by the tsunami of 1 April 1946.
Coast Guard buoy tender Clover established a temporary unmanned light within two weeks.
Present tower per the Society's record: concrete, skeletal.

notes_for_editor:
Wave height is disputed: 90 ft (Navy figure in the Daily Alaska Empire, 5 April 1946), over 100 ft (1999 Congressional Record), 130 ft (Rozell 2015), well over 120 ft (National Coast Guard Museum 2024). Times differ: the Nome Nugget's early Seattle dispatch gives 5:30 a.m. PST; Sanford's memo, quoted by Rozell and by the museum, gives 2:18 a.m. Cause: Rozell reports the older view that the earthquake raised the wave and a USGS finding of a submarine landslide that may have done so; the story states both without choosing.
Commissioner of Lighthouses reports: fiscal years and titles come from the corpus labels for bound volume bub_gb_B2dYAAAAYAAJ (fiscal 1915-1922). The 1917 citation gives the scan page only. The 1918, 1920 and 1921 printed pages were read from the OCR page index; check the page images before publishing. Titles follow the corpus label, not a title page read.
Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1931: the fog list follows the account of the year ending 30 June 1930; the story says so, but the year the list covers is inferred from layout.
Roster: 129 lines from the USLHS archive (NARA keeper registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory), person slugs from roster.py --json, roles normalised by roster.py. Coast Guard crew lines of 1941-1971 (role_raw USCG) carry no rating in the archive and are stored as role crew. Thomas A. Hill, Jr. is listed for 1945-1946 and is not named among the five dead; confirm before any page names him. Petit's rating comes from the 1999 Congressional Record.
Not used, worth a human look: Wikipedia leads for a 1909 Columbia cannery-ship wreck, a 1930 Koshun Maru wreck, a 1942 Turksib wreck, and a 1971 automation date. Newspaper searches for 1909 and 1942 returned nothing usable. None of these is in the story or the JSON.
Could not read: the USCG Historian's Scotch Cap page (archived copies returned no text), and mycg.uscg.mil (403). The Coast Guard Light List entry (LLNR 6-1220) was not read, so the lit or unlit status is not settled. The story says the sources disagree.
The item record calls the lens a Fresnel; the Society's record says first order bivalve. The story uses the Society's wording.
The record's structures entry (tower, concrete, wood, built 1903, standing) is corrected in corrections. The 1903 tower's later fate is not given in the sources read.
Photos: none added; the museum and Commons photos were not checked for licence.
Fact-check 2026-10-27: the 1923 Lighthouse Service Bulletin (source 14) is added. It says the Cape Sarichef and Scotch Cap stations exchanged code messages with the naval radio station at Dutch Harbor, which conflicts with the 1999 tribute's 'only contact' wording; the story states both. It also confirms the 1921 radio telephone installation. The museum says the radio station crew stayed until the end of April; Rozell says most of the men left within days; the story states both. The Nome Nugget dispatch gives 5:30 a.m. Pacific time; the story says so.
